You are a helpful chemistry assistant. You build 3D molecular
  structures from the chemical information you are given, including 2D drawings
  supplied as images.

  When you are given a 2D drawing of a molecule, your task is to produce the 3D
  structure that drawing depicts and save it as `answer.xyz` in your working
  directory.

  Requirements for `answer.xyz`:
  - Include all explicit hydrogens.
  - Use a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system, units of angstroms.
  - Standard XYZ format: first line is the total atom count, second line a
    one-line comment, each remaining line `Element X Y Z`.

  When you are done, confirm that `answer.xyz` exists in the working directory.

A 2D structure of a molecule is provided as a PNG file in your working directory: mol_0044.png

Build the 3D structure it depicts and save it as answer.xyz.

args.command:
cat << 'EOF' > b.py
from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem import AllChem
L1="O/C(C(F)(F)F)=C\\c%s:c:c:c:c:n:%s"
smi="Cl[Ge]1 2(OC(C(F)(F)F)=Cc3ccccn->13)(OC(C(F)(F)F)=Cc4ccccn->24)[Au]<-[Ge]5 6(OC(C(F)(F)F)=Cc7ccccn->57)OC(C(F)(F)F)=Cc8ccccn->68"
smi=smi.replace(" ","")
m=Chem.MolFromSmiles(smi)
print(m.GetNumAtoms())
mh=Chem.AddHs(m)
from rdkit.Chem import rdDistGeom
ps=rdDistGeom.ETKDGv3(); ps.useRandomCoords=True; ps.randomSeed=7
print(AllChem.EmbedMolecule(mh,ps))
Chem.MolToXYZFile(mh,"init.xyz")
print(Chem.GetFormalCharge(mh))
EOF
python b.py

content:
I built the 3D structure and saved it as `answer.xyz` in the working directory (76 atoms, all hydrogens included, standard XYZ format).

**What the structure is:** a Cl–Ge–Au–Ge chain. Each germanium carries two chelating ligands. Each ligand binds through an enolate oxygen and a pyridine nitrogen, on a –O–C(CF₃)=CH–(2-pyridyl) backbone with the C=C set so the two donors can both reach the metal. The left germanium also carries the chloride, so it is six-coordinate and the right one is five-coordinate.

**How I built it:** RDKit couldn't represent the Ge←N dative bonds, so I generated the starting 3D geometry without them. I then optimised in two steps with xTB, a fast semi-empirical method (GFN-FF first, then GFN2), holding the metal bond lengths with restraints.

**Caveat:** the final metal bond lengths are imposed values I chose, not free minimum-energy results. Unrestrained, GFN2 broke two bonds to the right germanium: Au–Ge stretched to 3.16 Å and one Ge–O to 2.53 Å. A second run that restrained only the Au and right-hand N bonds was also unacceptable: one left-hand Ge–N went to 2.50 Å and one right-hand Ge–O to 3.48 Å. So I restrained all ten metal-to-ligand bonds except the Ge–Cl. Final values:

| Bond | Length (Å) |
|---|---|
| Ge–Au (both) | 2.42, 2.44 |
| Ge–O (all four) | 1.91–1.92 |
| Ge–N, left Ge | 2.20, 2.20 |
| Ge–N, right Ge | 2.11, 2.12 |
| Ge–Cl (not restrained) | 2.29 |

No two atoms are closer than 1.08 Å. The geometry is a sensible model of the drawing, but treat it as a constrained structure rather than an energy minimum.
